abstract: This article argues that URL links, largely abandoned as a web research object after the rise of platformization, remain valuable tools for cross-platform controversy mapping. Using the nearly decade-long debate over the construction of a shipping canal through the Vistula Spit in Poland as a case study, the author analyzes 21,756 Facebook posts and 133,814 tweets to show that links function as reliable controversy indicators but in platform-specific ways. The study bridges early digital methods with contemporary studies of platformization and CSCW research on socio-technical systems and platform affordances.
key_claims: URLs can serve as reliable, traceable indicators of how participants engage with a controversy, but in platform-specific ways.
On Twitter, links foreground political sentiment, alignment, and polarization, while on Facebook, links foreground protest mobilization and local organization.
These platform differences are explained by platform affordances, which structure not only the circulation of content but also its meaning within controversies.
Links are not neutral carriers of information but socio-technical artifacts (non-human actors/mediators in ANT terms) whose meaning depends on platform design.
A methodological return to link analysis is warranted as a tool for cross-platform controversy mapping that does not rely exclusively on discursive analysis.
methods: Mixed-methods approach grounded in controversy mapping (an empirical version of Actor-Network Theory) applied to a single digital object: URLs in posts about the Vistula Spit Canal.

Data collection across two platforms using identical keywords: Twitter via the university's Twitter API through the 4CAT program, and Facebook via CrowdTangle, covering 1 January 2016 to 3 February 2023.

Nested query design: a 'core collection' using bare, non-evaluative object-phrases (e.g., 'Przekop Mierzei Wiślanej') and an 'extended collection' adding terms drawn from both supporters' and opponents' discourse.
Final corpus of 21,756 Facebook posts and 133,814 tweets; quantitative analysis of frequency and distribution of digital objects (likes, shares, mentions, retweets, links).

Network analysis in Gephi connecting accounts sharing the same URLs, spatialized with Force-Atlas 2, community detection via modularity-based (Louvain) clustering, and manual coding of link clusters into seven categories (news, local news, economic news, conservative sites, far-right sites, suspicious websites, informational sites), with political-leaning labels drawing on Media Bias/Fact Check and Wikipedia.
findings: On Twitter, external linking was among the most frequent activities (48.7% core, 61.8% extended), and links in the extended, retweet-dominated layer were markedly self-referential (about 52% pointed back to Twitter versus 31% in the core).

Twitter link networks in the extended collection were dense and polarized, concentrating around conservative, far-right, and suspicious (including Russian-language) clusters set against a news cluster, bridged mainly by self-referential platform-internal links—suggesting links signal political alignment rather than evidence.

On Facebook, over 90% of posts contained links (93% core, 94% extended) regardless of collection, a near-universal default despite the platform's 2018 algorithmic deprioritization of external-publisher content; link posts drew more comments than link-free posts (means of 20–26 vs. 15–17).

Facebook link clusters were more dispersed and oriented outward, linking to local news, environmental/pro-environmental groups, and grassroots protest accounts—functioning evidentially and as mobilizing resources.

The same resource type (mainstream news portals) was mobilized by different political camps across platforms (e.g., state broadcaster TVP circulated within Twitter's conservative/nationalist segment, while news portals on Facebook were shared by center/left-leaning accounts).
Post volume on both platforms tracked key stages of the controversy (2019 construction tender, 2020 cost increase and environmental decision, September 2022 canal opening).
contributions: Demonstrates empirically that URLs can serve as cross-platform controversy indicators that reveal how participants engage with contested issues in platform-specific ways.
Shows that platform affordances shape not only the circulation but also the meaning and function of links within controversies.
Argues for and revives a methodological return to link analysis as a tool for cross-platform controversy mapping, bridging early digital methods with platformization studies and CSCW.

Reframes links as active socio-technical mediators (non-human actors) rather than residual or neutral artifacts, and offers link-based trace analysis as a complement to discursive/semantic analysis for studying contested issues and potentially misinformation.
framing: The paper positions itself at the intersection of controversy mapping (an empirical version of Actor-Network Theory), web/digital methods studies of platformization and affordances, and CSCW research on socio-technical systems. It engages a conversation about how digital infrastructures and platform design mutually shape social practices, arguing for the renewed relevance of links as traceable artifacts amid tooling that privileges keywords, hashtags, and platform-native metrics.
